notes: Slice 'concepts': the ideas of privacy (9 concept cards), an 18-regime comparison matrix (jurisdictions), 13 cases where records were turned on people (harms), and 8 popular myths. Method: every quote was captured with tools/fetch-text.py and checked with --check (FOUND) before being marked CONFIRMED; non-English quotes are given in the original with translations in note. Primary texts were preferred (statutes on official portals: publications.europa.eu Cellar for EUR-Lex texts, legislation.gov.uk, uscode.house.gov, govinfo.gov, Texas/Colorado legislature sites, camara.leg.br, npc.gov.cn, meity.gov.in, KLRI, sso.agc.gov.sg, legislation.gov.au, gov.za, ndpc.gov.ng, odpc.go.ke, fedlex; judgments from the BVerfG, Library of Congress U.S. Reports and the Third Circuit). Where a publisher blocked scripted access (EUR-Lex, consilium.europa.eu, projectvrm.org, some law-review repositories) an official mirror or an Internet Archive snapshot was used and the note says so. Field conventions: jurisdictions add 'automatedSignalsProvision' (the provision behind the yes/partial/no rating) and optional 'notes'; concepts add 'displayDate' and 'locationNote'. 'automatedSignals' = 'yes' only where the law obliges controllers to honour a person's automated or machine-readable objection/opt-out; 'partial' for registry-style opt-outs (Do Not Call lists) or consent intermediaries (India's Consent Managers). Known gaps and caveats: Westin's 1967 definition is quoted via Margulis (2003) because the book is in copyright; Nissenbaum is quoted from the 2004 pre-publication manuscript; Solove from a university-hosted copy of the published article. Unverified or approximate: CCPA's 1 Jan 2020 operative date, APPI's 2003/2005 dates and PIPA's 2011 entry-into-force are standard dates not confirmed on a primary page; the Colorado $20,000 penalty is from a law-firm advisory; Korea's 2026 PIPA amendment is from IAPP (secondary); the EU 'data omnibus' (proposed GDPR Art. 88b on machine-readable signals) was still in negotiation — its status at Sept 2026 was not verified from a primary source; Brazil's PL 2338/2023 status after March 2025 not verified. Harms not included for lack of a readable primary source: OPM breach 2015 (House Oversight report PDF is image-only beyond page 1), Grindr's 2018 sharing of HIV status (press only), Clearview AI fines by EU DPAs/ICO (sites blocked or pages withdrawn), the 23andMe Chapter 11 sale (company investor site blocked), Robodebt (Royal Commission site blocked), Target pregnancy-prediction anecdote (single anonymous source in a paywalled NYT article — treated as unverified and left out). The NYT AOL article is listed as PENDING (paywall, HTTP 403).

concepts.originator: The Hippocratic Oath (author unknown; traditionally attributed to Hippocrates and the medical school of Kos)

concepts.definition: Whatever I see or hear in the lives of my patients, whether in connection with my professional practice or not, which ought not to be spoken of outside, I will keep secret, as considering all such things to be private.

sources.quote: Virtually nothing is known of the first physician named Hippocrates, but there are considered to have been several, all of them teachers at the famous medical school on the Mediterranean island of Cos. issues: The 'originator' field states an authorship claim as fact: 'Hippocratic school of Kos'. Modern scholars do not attribute the Oath to Hippocrates. Proposed dates range from the 5th to the 3rd century BCE, and one line of argument (Edelstein) gives it a Pythagorean origin. The NLM page only says the Oath 'may have marked' a move to train people outside 'the Asclepiads of Kos'. The locationNote already hedges ('authorship and exact date are unknown'), so the originator should hedge too.

The note on source[0] gives the date as 'late 5th or 4th century BCE'. That range is too narrow: estimates run from the 5th to the 3rd century BCE, including a Hellenistic dating. 'c. 400 BCE' is still an acceptable conventional displayDate.

concepts.name: Privacy as control over information

concepts.name: Informational self-determination
concepts.originator: Bundesverfassungsgericht, First Senate (Census Act judgment, BVerfGE 65, 1), which made it a constitutional right; the term 'informationelles Selbstbestimmungsrecht' goes back to Wilhelm Steinmüller and colleagues' 1971 expert report for the Federal Interior Ministry
concepts.place: Federal Constitutional Court, Karlsruhe, West Germany
concepts.definition: This fundamental right confers upon the individual the authority to, in principle, decide themselves on the disclosure and use of their personal data.

sources.title: Judgment of the First Senate of 15 December 1983, 1 BvR 209, 269, 362, 420, 440, 484/83 (Census Act) — official English translation
sources.quote: This fundamental right confers upon the individual the authority to, in principle, decide themselves on the disclosure and use of their personal data.

sources.institution: Bundesverfassungsgericht (Federal Constitutional Court of Germany)
sources.title: Judgment of the First Senate of 15 December 1983, 1 BvR 209/83 et al. (Census Act) — official English translation
sources.quote: A societal order, and its underlying legal order, would not be compatible with the right to informational self-determination if citizens were no longer able to tell who knows what kind of personal information about them, at what time and on which occasion.

sources.title: BVerfGE 65, 1 – Volkszählung
sources.quote: Das Grundrecht gewährleistet insoweit die Befugnis des Einzelnen, grundsätzlich selbst über die Preisgabe und Verwendung seiner persönlichen Daten zu bestimmen.

sources.institution: Deutscher Bundestag, Drucksache VI/3826, Anlage 1 (expert report for the Federal Ministry of the Interior)
sources.title: W. Steinmüller, B. Lutterbeck, C. Mallmann, U. Harbort, G. Kolb, J. Schneider, 'Grundfragen des Datenschutzes'
sources.quote: Prüfungsmaßstab, an dem öffentliche Informationsverarbeitung zu messen ist, so ergab sich oben 2., ist das informationelle Selbstbestimmungsrecht über das eigene Person- bzw. Gruppenbild
sources.note: --check FOUND. Translation: 'The standard against which public information processing is to be measured, as shown in 2. above, is the right of informational self-determination over one's own image as a person or group.' The Drucksache is the Interior Minister's answer of 7 September 1972. Its cover text says Steinmüller (Regensburg) was commissioned in December 1970 and that 'Das sehr umfangreiche Gutachten liegt seit Juli 1971 vor' (--check FOUND). The title page of Anlage 1 is dated 'Juli 1971'; its OCR reads 'C. Malimann' for Christoph Mallmann.

issues: The originator field credits the concept wholly to the Bundesverfassungsgericht. The court made informational self-determination a constitutional right in 1983, but it did not coin the idea or the term. The 'informationelle Selbstbestimmungsrecht' appears in the July 1971 expert report 'Grundfragen des Datenschutzes' by Wilhelm Steinmüller, Bernd Lutterbeck, Christoph Mallmann and others for the Federal Interior Ministry. That report was printed as Anlage 1 to Bundestag Drucksache VI/3826 (7 September 1972). German Wikipedia ('Informationelle Selbstbestimmung') also says the term goes back to this 1971 report. A primary source is added.

jurisdictions.automatedSignalsProvision: Art. 21(5): in information-society services the data subject 'may exercise his or her right to object by automated means using technical specifications'. The Commission's Digital Omnibus proposal (COM(2025) 837, 19 Nov 2025) would add Art. 88b. It covers processing in people's terminal equipment (the cookie rules). Controllers' online interfaces would have to let people give consent, refuse it, and object to direct marketing (Art. 21(2)) 'through automated and machine-readable means', and would have to respect those choices, from 24 months after entry into force. European standards would be requested to interpret the signals. Web browsers from providers that are not SMEs would have to supply the technical means after 48 months. On 23 Sept 2026 the proposal (2025/0360(COD)) was still at committee stage in the European Parliament ('Awaiting committee decision').
jurisdictions.aiRules: AI Act, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (general application 2 Aug 2026). The 'Digital omnibus on AI' was adopted by the Council on 29 June 2026 and published as Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (OJ L, 24 July 2026). It moved high-risk obligations to 2 Dec 2027 for stand-alone systems and 2 Aug 2028 for AI embedded in products. GDPR Art. 22 separately limits decisions based solely on automated processing.

issues: All seven quotes re-fetched and FOUND except source 6 (see below). Adoption 27 Apr 2016, OJ L 119 of 4 May 2016, application from 25 May 2018, Art. 83(5) fine ceiling, Art. 21(5), Art. 22(1) and AI Act Art. 113 all check out.

automatedSignalsProvision misdescribed proposed Art. 88b in three ways. (1) The article is limited by its title to 'processing of personal data in the terminal equipment of natural persons' (the cookie/ePrivacy rules moved into the GDPR). The summary presented it as a general machine-readable consent-and-objection duty. (2) The objection it covers is only the Art. 21(2) direct-marketing objection. (3) 'Once standards exist' comes from the explanatory memorandum. The operative text applies paragraphs 1-2 from a fixed date, 24 months after entry into force. Standards are requested separately and only give a presumption of conformity.

The record left out the part of Art. 88b that matters most for the MyTerms story: para. 6 would oblige web-browser providers that are not SMEs to provide the technical means for these machine-readable signals, 48 months after entry into force.

The record flagged the omnibus status as 'not independently verified'. The EP Legislative Observatory (fetched 23 Sept 2026) shows procedure 2025/0360(COD) at 'Awaiting committee decision': rapporteurs were appointed 25 Feb 2026 and the procedure has no committee vote yet. aiRules is correct. It can now name the final act: OEIL records Council adoption on 29/06/2026, signature on 08/07/2026 and publication as Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 in OJ L of 24.07.2026.

issues: The consequence says 'liquidated damages of $2,500 per violation'. The statute (18 U.S.C. 2710(c)(2)(A)) says 'actual damages but not less than liquidated damages in an amount of $2,500'. It does not say 'per violation', and $2,500 is a floor, not a fixed sum. Whether it applies per violation or per plaintiff is a question of judicial interpretation that the sources do not settle.

The consequence also calls the Act 'still one of the few U.S. laws protecting a specific kind of consumer record'. No source supports this, and it is contestable: the U.S. has many sectoral record-privacy statutes, including FCRA 1970, FERPA 1974, RFPA 1978, the Cable Act 1984, DPPA 1994, HIPAA 1996, COPPA 1998 and GLBA 1999. The clause should go.

myths.claim: Privacy is a modern invention — people in the past did not expect it.
myths.correction: The legal phrase 'right to privacy' is a 19th-century coinage, but the expectations behind it are far older: the Hippocratic Oath binds the physician to keep secret what he sees and hears in patients' lives, and English courts in 1604 held that a man's house is his 'Castle and Fortress', limiting even the sheriff's entry.

myths.claim: If you have nothing to hide, you have nothing to fear.
myths.correction: Privacy harms are not limited to exposing wrongdoing. Germany's Constitutional Court held in 1983 that people who fear being recorded stop exercising their rights; Solove's taxonomy counts chilled behaviour and shifts of power as harms; and the Church Committee found the FBI's COINTELPRO went 'far beyond' anyone involved in violence.
